name: The Clausius-Clapeyron Relation
statement: The slope of a phase-boundary line is set by the latent heat and the volume change.
statementAccent: the latent heat and the volume change
meaning: The relation describes how steeply a phase-coexistence line (where, say, liquid and vapour are in equilibrium) rises in a pressure-temperature diagram. The exact Clapeyron equation sets that slope equal to the latent heat of the transition divided by the temperature times the volume change between the phases. For a liquid and its vapour, a common approximation turns this into a simple exponential rise of vapour pressure with temperature.
mechanism: Along a coexistence line the two phases are in equilibrium, so their molar Gibbs free energies are equal, and they must change equally as one moves along the line. Applying the thermodynamic relation for how free energy changes with temperature and pressure to each phase and equating them gives the slope directly: the latent heat over the temperature times the volume change. This derivation uses no approximation, which is why the exact Clapeyron equation is completely general. The Clausius-Clapeyron approximation adds the assumptions that the vapour is an ideal gas and the condensed phase's volume is negligible, yielding the exponential vapour-pressure form.

examples.text: Because vapour pressure rises with temperature, lower air pressure means a lower boiling point, so water boils below a hundred degrees on a mountain, near seventy at the summit of Everest.
Water expands on freezing, so the volume change of melting is negative and the ice-water line slopes backward: raising the pressure lowers the melting point, a rare and telling exception.
The relation gives the rule that the atmosphere can hold roughly seven per cent more water vapour per degree of warming, a thermodynamic benchmark behind expectations of heavier extreme rainfall.

variants.name: The exact Clapeyron equation
variants.text: The general form, slope equal to latent heat over temperature times volume change, valid for any two-phase boundary (melting, vaporisation, or sublimation) given the latent heat and volume-change data.

variants.name: The Clausius-Clapeyron approximation
variants.text: The liquid-vapour special case that assumes ideal-gas vapour and negligible liquid volume, giving vapour pressure rising exponentially and integrating to a logarithm of the pressure ratio.

whyItMatters: It is the fundamental relation governing phase transitions in a pressure-temperature diagram, connecting the latent heat of a transition to the shape of its coexistence curve. It explains how boiling points shift with pressure, lets vapour pressures be predicted from latent heats, and supplies the Clausius-Clapeyron scaling that underlies climate reasoning about atmospheric moisture and extreme precipitation.

working.text: for any phase boundary, take the slope as latent heat over temperature times volume change, given the two phases' data.
for a liquid and its vapour, use the exponential Clausius-Clapeyron form to relate vapour pressure and temperature over modest ranges.

working.lead: Read the sign of the slope
working.text: note that a negative volume change, as in water freezing, tilts the coexistence line backward, so pressure lowers the transition temperature.

limits: The exact Clapeyron equation is general but needs the latent heat and volume change as data. The Clausius-Clapeyron approximation rests on three assumptions (ideal-gas vapour, negligible condensed-phase volume, and constant latent heat) all of which degrade over wide temperature ranges and fail entirely near the critical point, where the volume change and latent heat both vanish. The integrated logarithmic form is accurate only over modest intervals. And the seven-per-cent-per-degree figure bounds atmospheric moisture capacity, not actual rainfall, which scales differently by region and storm type.
misreadings: The Clausius-Clapeyron and Clapeyron equations are not the same: the Clapeyron form is exact and general, while the Clausius-Clapeyron form is the approximate liquid-vapour special case, and its exponential form does not apply to melting lines. The pressure-melting of ice is real but far too small to be the main reason skates glide, which owes more to a surface quasi-liquid layer and frictional heating. And the moisture-capacity figure is a bound on vapour, not a guaranteed rate for precipitation.
origin: Derived in its exact form by Benoit Paul Emile Clapeyron in 1834 and placed on a firm thermodynamic footing by Rudolf Clausius around 1850, who developed the ideal-gas approximation for the vapour branch.

sources.text: Clausius, R. (1850). “Ueber die bewegende Kraft der Wärme und die Gesetze, welche sich daraus für die Wärmelehre selbst ableiten lassen.” Annalen der Physik, vol. 155. — Clausius's paper, which puts Clapeyron's 1834 relation on a thermodynamic footing.
